question: What is the medical term for dangerously high blood sugar?
explanation: Hyperglycemia just means too much glucose floating in the blood. You've got this! Keep building that nursing vocabulary. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why do nurses check blood sugar in patients without known diabetes who suddenly become confused?

options.A: To rule out abnormal blood sugar as the cause

explanation: Changes in blood sugar can mess with brain function quickly. Checking it helps you figure out if confusion is coming from a high or low glucose level! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h1)

question: Which part of the glucometer setup has the chemical reagents that react with blood?
explanation: The test strip does the heavy lifting! It contains special enzymes that react with the glucose in the blood sample. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h2)

question: How does a glucometer turn a drop of blood into a number on the screen?

options.A: By taking a photo of the blood drop
options.B: By sensing the skin temperature of the finger
options.C: By measuring the electrical current from a chemical reaction

explanation: When blood hits the strip, a tiny electrical current is produced. The meter reads this current and turns it into the number you see! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h2)

question: A patient on a continuous insulin drip in the ward needs which type of monitoring?

options.A: Testing only when they feel thirsty
options.B: A fasting test once a week
options.C: Capillary checks once a month at home

explanation: Insulin drips lower blood sugar fast! Regular checks keep the patient safe from sudden crashes. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h3)

question: Which signs should make a nurse check a patient's blood sugar right away?

options.A: Lower back pain and dark urine
options.B: Swollen ankles and shortness of breath

explanation: These are classic signs of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Grab your glucometer and check them right away! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h3)

question: Why must you check the expiration date on test strips before using them?

options.A: Expired strips contain degraded chemicals that give wrong readings
options.B: Expired strips can damage the meter port
options.D: Expired strips turn bright red in the air

explanation: The chemicals on test strips break down over time. Always check the date so your readings are trustworthy! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h4)

question: What is the primary reason for warming a patient's hand before obtaining a capillary blood sample?

options.A: To thoroughly sterilize the skin surface without using alcohol
options.B: To numb the nerve endings so the skin puncture feels painless
options.C: To increase local blood flow and get a good drop easily
options.D: To dry away excessive sweat that could dilute the blood sample

explanation: Warming dilates local blood vessels, ensuring a rich droplet of capillary blood without needing excessive finger squeezing. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why should you wipe away the very first drop of blood after a finger prick?

options.A: The first drop contains tissue fluid that dilutes the sample
options.B: The first drop has too many red blood cells
options.C: The first drop causes a meter error code
options.D: The first drop is full of dirt

explanation: Tissue fluid mixes into that very first drop and can make your glucose reading falsely low. Wiping it away gives you a clean sample! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h5)

question: Where is the best spot on the finger to prick for a blood sample?

options.A: The direct center of the finger pad
options.B: The base of the fingernail bed
options.C: The soft skin right over the joint

explanation: The sides of our fingertips have fewer nerve endings than the pads, making the prick much less painful for your patient. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h5)

question: Which fasting blood sugar reading is normal for an adult without diabetes?
explanation: A normal fasting blood sugar usually falls between 70 and 99 mg/dL. You're doing great learning these vital signs! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h6)

question: What immediate action should a nurse take when a patient's glucometer reading returns a value of 50 mg/dL?

options.A: Encourage the patient to exercise vigorously to burn off remaining sugars
options.B: Withhold all future meals until a fasting blood panel is drawn tomorrow
options.C: Document the finding and schedule a re-test during the next routine shift
options.D: Administer fast-acting oral carbohydrates or follow the low blood sugar protocol

explanation: A value of 50 mg/dL indicates hypoglycemia, which requires immediate treatment to raise the blood glucose safely. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h6)

question: When do you need to run a quality control check with liquid control solution?

options.B: When opening a new container of test strips

explanation: Whenever you crack open a new batch of strips, run a control test to make sure your meter and the new strips agree. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h7)

question: What should you do if your control solution test result falls way outside the normal range?

options.A: Use the meter on patients anyway and note the variance
options.B: Ignore the test because controls are unreliable
options.C: Add water to the control solution
options.D: Take the meter out of service and report it

explanation: If the control check fails, the system isn't reliable. Put it aside and report the equipment issue so patient safety isn't compromised. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h7)

question: A patient is shaking and sweating, but the meter reads 120 mg/dL. What is your best next step?

options.A: Assume the meter is right and ignore the symptoms
options.B: Repeat the test or consider a lab check

explanation: Always trust your clinical instincts! If the patient's symptoms don't match the number, recheck to be certain. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h8)

question: Which of these is a common cause of an inaccurate glucometer reading?

options.A: Using too little blood on the test strip
options.B: Pricking the side of the finger
options.C: Wiping the outside of the meter clean

explanation: The strip needs enough blood to fill the reaction zone. If the sample is too small, the meter might give an error or a false reading. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h8)

question: Where should used lancets go immediately after a finger prick?

options.B: In a rigid, puncture-proof sharps container
options.D: In a clean kidney basin to wash later

explanation: Safety first! Used sharps go straight into a puncture-resistant container to protect everyone from accidental sticks. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h9)

question: Why is it strictly forbidden to use a single-patient lancing device on more than one person?

options.B: It can transmit serious bloodborne infections
options.C: It melts the plastic body of the device
options.D: It causes an internal meter error

explanation: Tiny traces of blood stay on lancing equipment. Sharing devices is a huge infection risk—always use a fresh device per patient! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T5#GNS212_U4_T5_h9)
